wording_corrections.old: Use the concrete case as the shared normal case and the independent question as a second case. Each pair creates a boundary or missing-information case and predicts its result before testing. Keep the expected result separate from an observed mistake.
wording_corrections.new: Use the supplied two-by-two decoder and declared averaging rule for shared practice. Keep original and blurred grids with the calculations. Reserve the new two-by-four equal-count pair for the individual first attempt; do not use it as a paired investigation.

wording_corrections.old: Keep for an independent attempt: Use 0 for dark and 1 for light. Draw a two-by-two image with rows [1,0] and [0,1]. Then change only the bottom-left pixel to light. Which number changes?
wording_corrections.new: Keep the reversed-colour two-by-two question for optional later practice. Reserve the new two-by-four equal-count pair for the first independent attempt before feedback.
Additional transfer practice: a different colour convention

wording_corrections.old: Complete this after teaching and guided practice have ended.
wording_corrections.new: Use this checklist after practice. The new two-by-four equal-count pair is this week’s selected independent attempt.

wording_corrections.old: REQUIRED PROOF  Decode a 4 by 4 number grid, identify the pictured shape, then predict which details disappear when neighboring cells are averaged.
wording_corrections.new: EXPLANATION CHECK  State dimensions, reading order and the colour convention; reconstruct the values and explain which spatial information a count discards.

wording_corrections.old: MODEL REASONING Each grid position becomes one displayed square. A blur combines nearby values, so isolated corners and thin lines disappear before large regions. The computer transforms numbers; the human viewer recognizes the shape.
wording_corrections.new: Each grid position becomes one displayed square. A blur combines values according to a chosen procedure; details may become less distinct depending on that procedure and the picture. Our investigation declares a specific averaging rule so its result can be traced exactly. Reconstructing or transforming numbers does not by itself recognise what the picture depicts.
